beats: You ask a chatbot to plan a trip, and it gives you a nice list.
You ask an AI agent, and it actually goes and checks the flights, compares the prices, and puts the booking on your calendar.
Same kind of AI underneath. So what's the difference?
By the end of this video, you'll understand exactly how AI agents work. No jargon, no hype. Let's get into it.
Let's start with the thing you already know: a chatbot. You type a message, the model reads it, and it writes back.
One question, one answer. Then it stops and waits for you.
An agent is different in one important way: it doesn't stop after one answer.
You give it a goal, and it keeps working. Taking steps, checking results, and deciding what to do next, until the goal is done, or until it needs your help.
Anthropic, the company behind Claude, defines agents as systems where LLMs, large language models, dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage.
In plain English: the AI decides the steps, not a fixed script.
Almost every AI agent is built from the same four parts.
One: the brain. That's a large language model, like GPT, Gemini or Claude. It reads the situation and decides what to do next.
Two: tools. On its own, a language model can only produce text. Tools give it hands: a web search, a calculator, a calendar, a code runner, a browser.
The model doesn't press the buttons itself. It writes a short, structured request, like: search the web for flights from London to New York on Friday.
And the software around it runs that tool and hands back the result.
Three: memory. Agents keep track of what's happened so far: the goal, the steps they've taken, and what they've learned.
Short-term memory is the running conversation. Long-term memory can be notes or a database the agent can search later.
And four: the loop. This is the part that turns a chatbot into an agent.
The loop is simple: think, act, observe, repeat.
This idea was popularised by a 2022 research paper called ReAct, short for reasoning and acting, from researchers at Princeton and Google.
They showed that letting a model alternate between reasoning about a problem and taking actions works better than doing either one alone.
Let's watch it run. Say your goal is: find a highly rated ramen place open after 10 p.m. near me, and send the details to my friend.
Think: the agent reasons, first I need ramen places nearby that are open late.
Act: it calls the search tool.
Observe: it reads the results. Five places. Two close at nine.
Think again: three options left. I should check the ratings.
Act: another search. Observe: one has four point seven stars.
Think: good, now send it. Act: it calls the messaging tool. Observe: message sent.
Goal complete. The loop ends.
Notice that nobody wrote those steps in advance. The model chose each step based on what it had just seen.
That's the whole trick, and it's why agents can handle messy, real-world tasks.
Now, not everything called an agent really is one.
Many AI products are actually workflows: the steps are fixed in code, and the AI fills in one part, like: summarise this email, then file it.
That's predictable, cheap, and often exactly what you want.

For example, a support workflow might always do the same three steps: read the ticket, look up the order, draft a reply. An agent given the same ticket might decide it first needs to check the delivery status, or ask the customer a question.
A true agent chooses its own path. That makes it more flexible, but also slower, more expensive, and harder to predict.
Anthropic's own advice to developers is to start with the simplest solution, and only add agent-like freedom when the task really needs it.
That's a useful rule for you too, when you're judging a new AI tool.
So why isn't everything an agent already? Because each loop is another chance to go wrong.
If the model misreads a result early, every later step builds on that mistake.
Agents can get stuck repeating the same action. Long tasks can burn through a lot of computing cost.
And there's a security risk called prompt injection: a web page or email can contain hidden instructions, and an agent that reads it might try to follow them.
That's why good agents ask for confirmation before doing anything you can't undo, like paying, deleting or sending.
Even the analysts are cautious. Gartner predicts that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027, because of rising costs, unclear value or weak risk controls.
At the same time, it expects at least 15% of day-to-day work decisions to be made autonomously by agentic AI by 2028, up from zero in 2024.
Big promise, real growing pains.
Let's recap. An AI agent is a language model with four parts: a brain that decides, tools that act, memory that keeps track,
and a loop: think, act, observe, repeat, that keeps going until the goal is done.
So next time a company says its product is agentic, ask two questions: does it choose its own steps, and does it check with you before it does something it can't undo?

short: An AI agent isn't a smarter chatbot. It's a loop.
A chatbot answers once, and stops.
An agent gets a goal, then repeats three steps. Think: what should I do next?
Act: use a tool, like web search, a calendar, or a browser.
Observe: read the result. Then it loops again, and again, until the job is done.
Researchers call this pattern ReAct: reasoning plus acting.
That's how AI can research, book and code on its own.
